where: lesson hh, question 1 (PCO₂ 20, HCO₃⁻ 12 → pH 7.40), explanation
what: The explanation says the gas is 'a heavily compensated metabolic acidosis, or a mixed disorder'. By the app's own Winter's rule the expected PCO₂ for HCO₃⁻ 12 is 1.5×12+8 = 26 ± 2 (24–28), so a PCO₂ of 20 is too low: this cannot be a compensated metabolic acidosis. Compensation also never brings pH back to 7.40. This is the step the 'learn' lesson says learners get wrong most often (47%), and here the app teaches the wrong habit.
evidence: Run node: Winter 1.5*12+8 = 26. Answering Q1 in lesson hh shows the explanation (screenshot /tmp/claude-0/-home-claude/80312b5f-0e45-5589-b131-fcf824f33899/scratchpad/beta/shots/T02-hh-answered-desk.png).
fix: Replace the explanation with: '12 ÷ (0.03 × 20) = 20, the normal ratio, so pH 7.40. A normal pH with both values far from normal is never compensation alone: Winter's predicts PCO₂ 26 ± 2, so 20 means a second disorder (metabolic acidosis plus respiratory alkalosis, e.g. salicylate or sepsis).'

what: Says SpO₂ targets 'sit at 92–96% for most patients'. The cited UK guideline (BTS 2017, already in SRC as odriscoll17) and every other place in the app (c2.js:177, c3.js:275, c10.js:51, c12.js:77, ui6.js:43, c8.js:51) say 94–98%. A learner preparing for MRCEM gets two different numbers.
evidence: grep '92–96\|94–98' c*.js ui*.js; O'Driscoll BR et al. BTS guideline for oxygen use in adults. Thorax 2017;72(Suppl 1):ii1–ii90 (target 94–98%, 88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic failure).
fix: Change to 'SpO₂ targets sit at 94–98% for most acutely ill patients (88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure), BTS 2017'. Optionally add 'some guidelines (TSANZ 2015) use 92–96%'. Add odriscoll17 to LSRC.odc.

where: lesson microbes · question 2 (CML, WBC 280, PaO₂ 48, SpO₂ 98%)
what: The distractor 'Venous sample' is also a correct explanation: a venous sample gives PO₂ ~40–50 with a normal SpO₂ in a well patient. Two defensible answers.
evidence: Stem: 'A patient with CML (WBC 280) has PaO₂ 48 but SpO₂ 98% and looks well.' Nothing excludes venous sampling.
fix: Make the arterial sample certain in the stem, e.g. 'Arterial sample confirmed (pulsatile flash, PaCO₂ 38). A repeat analysed at once on ice reads PaO₂ 92.' Or replace the 'Venous sample' option with 'Pulmonary embolism'.

where: Lesson check questions (L[].q from c1–c4 and XQ in c6–c8) · exam style
what: The check questions do not match the exams this learner is sitting. 487 of 490 have 4 options (MRCEM SBA and USMLE use 5 or more). The median stem is 52 characters and none is 150 characters or longer, so none is a clinical vignette. Many distractors are implausible ('It replaces the need for sleep', 'Give bicarbonate' / 'Ignore it' for VBG PCO₂ 62, 'None; use urine'). Some questions repeat: DKA Q2 and Q5 and VBG Q1 all ask whether a venous sample is enough. These questions train recall, not the applied SBA reasoning both exams test.
evidence: page.evaluate over L[].q: n = 490, options {4: 487, 2: 3}, median stem 52 chars, p90 78, 0 stems ≥ 150. Lessons read: learn, vbg, dka.
fix: Rewrite at least the 2 lesson-end questions per clinical lesson (module 9 and 10) as 5-option vignettes: age, setting, obs and a full gas table in the stem, with homogeneous distractors (all disorders or all next steps). Drop the joke distractors. Remove the near-duplicates (c3.js dka q2/q5 and the vbg lesson q1).

what: Says 'The traditional (Boston) approach with albumin-corrected anion gap and base excess'. Base excess belongs to the Copenhagen approach (Siggaard-Andersen). The Boston approach is HCO₃⁻ plus the compensation rules. Mixing up these names in the module that introduces all three schools will confuse readers.
evidence: c1.js stewart body. The Boston school is Schwartz and Relman (bicarbonate plus empirical compensation rules); the Copenhagen school is Siggaard-Andersen (standard base excess); see Berend 2014 NEJM 371:1434.
fix: Rewrite: 'The bicarbonate (Boston) approach with an albumin-corrected anion gap, and the base-excess (Copenhagen) approach, give the same answers in almost every patient.' Cite a comparison study (e.g. Dubin A et al. Crit Care Med 2007;35:1264–1270) in LSRC.stewart.

what: Two distractors are the same step: 'Acidaemia versus alkalaemia' and 'Reading the pH'. In effect the question has three options, and a learner can rule out both by spotting the duplicate. The stem and the key also say 'audits' (plural) when the lesson cites one single-centre audit.
evidence: Lesson learn Q2 (screenshot /tmp/claude-0/-home-claude/80312b5f-0e45-5589-b131-fcf824f33899/scratchpad/beta/shots/T02-learn-desk.png). Keys: 'Weakest step in audits'.
fix: Replace 'Reading the pH' with 'Calculating the anion gap' (69% in the audit, a real near-miss). Change 'In audits of junior doctors' to 'In a 2024 audit of junior doctors' and the key to 'Weakest step (2024 audit)'.

what: The SID is written as 'Na⁺ + K⁺ + Ca²⁺ + Mg²⁺ − Cl⁻ − lactate' with no valence factor. The app uses mmol/L throughout. The next lesson (stewartx) and the concept-web node use 2·Ca and 2·Mg, so a learner using this formula with mmol/L values gets the wrong number.
evidence: Compare the c1 stewart body with c4 stewartx ('2·iCa + 2·Mg') and the ui5 WEB_NODES 'sid'.
fix: Write 'Na⁺ + K⁺ + 2×Ca²⁺ + 2×Mg²⁺ − Cl⁻ − lactate (mmol/L; ionised Ca and Mg)'.

what: 'D-lactate (bacterial) ... See the next lesson.' The next lesson is ketones; D-lactate is in microbes, two lessons on.
evidence: Order in L: lactate (12) → ketones (13) → microbes (14). The pager on lactate says 'Next: Ketones and ketoacidosis'.
fix: Change to 'See "Microbes, the gut and the syringe" later in this module', ideally as a link: <a href="#l-microbes">.

what: 'Each mmol consumes one HCO₃⁻, which the kidneys must regenerate. That is the whole job of renal acid excretion.' This leaves out reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate (≈ 4,000–4,500 mmol/day), which is most of the kidney's acid–base work and the basis of proximal RTA, taught later.
evidence: Rose & Post ch. 11; GFR 180 L/day × 24 mmol/L ≈ 4,300 mmol/day filtered.
fix: Replace the last sentence with: 'The kidney has two jobs: reclaim nearly all of the ≈ 4,300 mmol of bicarbonate filtered each day (proximal tubule), and make new bicarbonate to replace what fixed acid used up (ammonium and titratable acid excretion).'

where: lesson acidsrc · 'The two clocks' vs question 5
what: The section is called 'The two clocks' (lungs, kidneys) but question 5 asks to order three responses including buffers, which the lesson never mentions.
evidence: Body has no mention of chemical buffering; q5 answer 'Buffers, lungs, kidneys'.
fix: Rename to 'Three clocks' and add: 'Chemical buffers (bicarbonate, haemoglobin, proteins, bone) act in seconds, lungs in minutes, kidneys over 3–5 days.' Add a key 'Buffers: seconds'.

what: The heading says three but the list has four bullets (diabetic, euglycaemic DKA, alcoholic, starvation).
fix: Rename to 'Four kinds of ketoacidosis', or nest euglycaemic DKA under diabetic and keep 'Three'.

where: lesson ketones · key 'Urine strip detects: Acetoacetate only'
what: Nitroprusside reacts with acetoacetate and (weakly) acetone; 'only' is wrong as stated. The teaching point is that it misses β-hydroxybutyrate.
evidence: Standard chemistry of nitroprusside strips (e.g. Laffel 1999 Diabetes Metab Res Rev 15:412).
fix: Key: 'Urine strip misses' → 'β-hydroxybutyrate'. Body: 'detect acetoacetate (and a little acetone), not BHB'.

what: States D-lactic acidosis gives 'a high anion gap acidosis'. D-lactate is excreted in urine faster than L-lactate, so the anion gap is often only mildly raised or even normal; a normal gap does not exclude it. (Doubt level: I am confident of this point but did not fetch the paper.)
evidence: Kowlgi NG, Chhabra L. D-lactic acidosis: an underrecognized complication of short bowel syndrome. Gastroenterol Res Pract 2015;2015:476215.
fix: Add: 'The gap may be only mildly raised, or normal, because the kidney excretes D-lactate quickly.' Add the source to SRC and LSRC.microbes.

what: 'A high venous saturation with a high lactate suggests cells cannot use oxygen: cyanide, late sepsis, or shunting.' A learner who has just read 'shunt' in the hypoxaemia lesson reads this as pulmonary shunt, which lowers venous saturation.
evidence: Body text of o2content; hypox lesson uses 'shunt' for pulmonary shunt.
fix: Write 'microcirculatory (arteriovenous) shunting, where blood bypasses the tissues'.

what: '"40-50-60 → 75-?-90"' — the '?' reads as a typo and the hook is not memorable. At 50 mmHg saturation is ≈ 85%.
evidence: Severinghaus 1966 equation: S(50 mmHg) ≈ 84–85%. The app's own ODC model shows ≈ 85% at 50.
fix: '40-50-60 → 75-85-90, and P50 is 27. Right shift releases; left shift hoards.' Optionally add 50 mmHg / 85% to the table.

what: 'the same PaCO₂ with pH 7.25 needs non-invasive ventilation' — BTS/ICS 2016 says start NIV when pH < 7.35 and PaCO₂ > 6.5 kPa persist after optimal medical therapy (and controlled oxygen), usually reassessed within about an hour; the guideline the lesson cites.
evidence: Davidson AC et al. BTS/ICS guideline, Thorax 2016;71(Suppl 2):ii1–ii35, recommendations for AECOPD.
fix: '...with pH 7.25 that persists after nebulisers, steroids and controlled oxygen (target 88–92%) needs NIV.'

where: lesson lactate · question 2 'Which lactate type is metformin toxicity?'
what: Options A/B1/B2/B3 are shuffled at render (seen as 'B3, A, B2, B1') and sit beside the A–D key letters, so the learner sees '[A] B3 · [B] A · [C] B2 · [D] B1'. Confusing to read and to tap.
fix: Write options as 'Type A', 'Type B1', etc., and add a per-question 'keep order' flag (e.g. 5th element {fixed:1}) that renderLesson in ui1.js honours for ordinal options.

what: Three app-meta 'facts' go into the Number flash deck: 'Weakest step in audits: Compensation (≈ 47% correct)', 'Reflex target: 90% correct, < 8 s' and 'Review spacing: 1·3·7·16·35 days'. These are not blood-gas knowledge, and the 47% is an unsourced statistic.
evidence: FLASH dump: ids learn-0, learn-1, learn-2.
fix: Exclude lesson 'learn' from FLASH in ui5.js (filter l.id!=='learn'), or tag lesson keys with noflash:true.

where: lessons dalton, alv, henry, o2content, odc, ratios, co2vent (c1); nph, npo2, nall (c2); tc-venous, tc-bubbles (c4); icu-* (c10); sp-alt, sp-elder, sp-dive (c11)
what: Lesson prose gives pressures in mmHg only, and inconsistently: some lessons pair them ('PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg (4.7–6.0 kPa)', respfail, asthma, copd), many do not (dalton has 28 mmHg mentions and no kPa; sp-alt has 14). A kPa user (the UK MRCEM standard) gets a mixed experience. Lesson text is static, so I am not proposing live conversion, but kPa-first readers need the equivalents.
evidence: Sweep with S.units='kPa' and openLesson(id) over all 98 lessons, counting mmHg vs kPa in innerText. Examples: dalton mmHg×28 kPa×6 (the 6 come from the embedded widget only); sp-alt ×14/0; sp-elder ×9/0; icu-rosc ×7/1.
fix: Add the kPa equivalent the first time each key number appears in a lesson ('PaO₂ 60 mmHg (8 kPa)'), as respfail already does, or use a {p:60} token that renders in S.units with the other unit in brackets. Same for c2/c4/c10/c11.

where: Lesson learn (How you will learn blood gases) · sources
what: The lesson rests on specific evidence: the Aswan University Hospital audit (2024, with percentages), Hatala 2003 (interleaving, ECG), expertise reversal, calibration and so on. Its only source is Berend NEJM 2014, which is about acid–base physiology, not teaching methods. This breaks the 'cite everything' rule. The audit is real: Cureus 2024, PMC11687335.
fix: Add LSRC entries for the Aswan audit (Cureus 2024;16:e74…, PMC11687335) and Hatala RM et al., Med Educ 2003 (interleaving ECG). Also cite Roediger & Karpicke 2006 (testing effect), Cepeda 2006 (spacing) and Kalyuga 2003 (expertise reversal).

what: Body: 'up to about 20 in the elderly', but age/4+4 gives 24 at 80 and 21 at 70. Q2's explanation uses the American spelling 'edema'; the brief requires British English ('oedema').
evidence: c1.js lesson alv; Q2 explanation 'Think PE, pneumonia, edema.'
fix: 'under 10 in the young, about 20–25 at 70–80'; 'oedema'.

where: lesson henry, question 2 option and explanation
what: The answer says 'About half of normal', but the explanation computes 8.2 vs ≈ 20 mL/dL (41%).
fix: Make the option 'Less than half of normal'.

what: '[H⁺] … roughly a million times lower than plasma sodium': 140 mmol/L ÷ 40 nmol/L = 3.5 million.
fix: 'about three and a half million times lower'.

where: lesson buffer body ('The bicarbonate system has a pKa of 6.1')
what: 6.1 is the apparent pK′ of the CO₂/HCO₃⁻ system (dissolved CO₂ standing in for H₂CO₃). Carbonic acid's own pKa is ≈ 3.5. Learners who meet '3.6' in chemistry texts will think one value is wrong, and the ca lesson says carbonic acid 'exists only fleetingly'.
fix: Add: '(6.1 is the apparent pK of CO₂ ⇌ HCO₃⁻; carbonic acid itself is much stronger, pKa ≈ 3.5, but exists only in tiny amounts)'.

what: 'Ammonia/ammonium' is listed among the buffers. NH₃/NH₄⁺ has a pKa of about 9.2, so it is not a useful buffer at body or urine pH. Its role is acid excretion through ammoniagenesis (the note says this, but the table title implies buffering).
fix: Note in the row: 'not a true buffer at urine pH (pKa 9.2); carries H⁺ out as NH₄⁺'.

what: 'Use FiO₂ as a fraction (0.21 → 0.21)' — the example maps a value to itself.
fix: 'Use FiO₂ as a fraction (21% → 0.21).'

where: lesson hypox · table row V/Q mismatch
what: 'COPD, asthma, pneumonia, PE (the commonest cause)' reads as 'PE is the commonest cause of hypoxaemia'.
fix: Move to the mechanism cell: 'V/Q mismatch (the commonest mechanism)'.

where: lesson toxalc · question 2 isopropanol, correct option
what: 'Ketosis without acidosis and an osmolar gap' can be read as 'without acidosis and without an osmolar gap'. Also it is the only long option, a length cue.
fix: 'Ketosis and an osmolar gap, but no acidosis'; lengthen distractors, e.g. 'Severe HAGMA with an osmolar gap'.

what: 'raises content from ≈ 8.8 to ≈ 12.6 mL/dL' — with SaO₂ 0.92 and PaO₂ 65: 1.34×10×0.92 + 0.003×65 = 12.5.
fix: Change 12.6 to 12.5.

what: 'PaCO₂ = 0.863 × VCO₂ ÷ V_A' has no units; 0.863 only works with VCO₂ in mL/min (STPD) and V_A in L/min (BTPS), PaCO₂ in mmHg.
fix: Add '(VCO₂ in mL/min, V_A in L/min, PaCO₂ in mmHg). Example: 200 ÷ 4.3 × 0.863 ≈ 40.'

what: 'In the Drill's step-by-step mode' — the Practice tab calls this mode 'Step by step'; 'Drill' is a different label (drill titles).
fix: 'In Practice → Step by step, some cases end with a "What happens next" step built on these numbers.' Make it a button to startSession('steps').

what: Body says 'Sulfuric acid', question 3 says 'Sulphuric acid'. Lactate body says 'citric acid cycle', lactate q5 says 'Krebs cycle'.
fix: Pick one spelling (UK medical texts and IUPAC use 'sulfuric') and one name ('citric acid (Krebs) cycle' once, then one).

what: Cyanide appears in both type A and type B2 rows without explanation.
fix: Keep it in B2 only (or A only) and add a note: 'Cyanide and CO block cell use of oxygen, so they straddle A and B.'

what: In 5 of 65 questions the correct option is the only long one (acidsrc q2, ketones q2, toxalc q2, co2vent q2, ventchg q3), a give-away for test-wise learners.
evidence: Script: options where correct length > 1.5 × longest distractor.
fix: Lengthen distractors to match, e.g. ketones q2 'Insulin drives the liver to make more acetoacetate'.

what: 'WBC 280' has no unit.
'Urine strip detects: Acetoacetate only.' The nitroprusside strip also reacts weakly with acetone. The teaching point is that it misses BHB.
fix: Change it to 'Acetoacetate (and acetone), not BHB'.

where: lessons hh, alv, stewart (no worked gas)
what: None of the 12 lessons in start/chem/phys has a worked gas (ex), although hh (the Henderson consistency check) and alv (A–a) are exactly where a printout helps.
evidence: Learn module list shows no 'WORKED GAS' tag in modules 00–02.
fix: Add ex to hh (an internally inconsistent gas, e.g. pH 7.40, PCO₂ 60, HCO₃⁻ 24) and alv (an opioid overdose on room air, PaCO₂ 80, PaO₂ 48, age 30).

where: lesson buffer, open versus closed system
what: The claim 'a load of 10 mmol/L of strong acid would produce a severe acidosis' would stick far better with the numbers.
evidence: Closed: HCO₃⁻ 14, CO₂ 11.2 → pH 6.1 + log(14/11.2) = 6.20. Open (PCO₂ held at 40): pH 6.1 + log(14/1.2) = 7.17.
fix: Add a two-row table: closed beaker pH 6.20 versus open body pH 7.17 for the same 10 mmol/L acid load.

what: PiO₂ is given for Riyadh and Abha only. A 'your altitude' field in Settings would let the A–a and PiO₂ teaching (and the interpreter) use the learner's own site.
fix: Add S.altitude in Settings; show 'At your site: Patm ≈ X, PiO₂ ≈ Y' in dalton and alv and use it in interp.

what: The diffusion bullet suggests diffusion limitation commonly causes hypoxaemia. At rest it is the rarest of the mechanisms; it shows mainly on exercise and at altitude.
fix: Add: 'At rest, diffusion limitation alone rarely causes hypoxaemia; it shows on exercise or at altitude, when transit time shortens.'

what: None of these lessons has a worked gas (l.ex), while 23 clinical lessons do. ketones, toxalc, microbes, respfail and ventchg are ideal for one, and the 'Open in the Interpreter' button is the bridge from theory to practice.
fix: Add ex: ketones (euglycaemic DKA on empagliflozin: pH 7.18, PCO₂ 22, glu 11, BHB 5.2), toxalc (early: osm 322, AG 13), microbes (D-lactate: AG 24, lac 1.1), respfail (acute-on-chronic: pH 7.25, PCO₂ 80, HCO₃⁻ 34), ventchg (DKA before/after sedation).

what: The lesson says 'Calculate the A–a gradient' but never gives the alveolar gas equation or the app's normal (≤ age/4 + 4).
fix: Add a key 'Normal A–a ≤ age/4 + 4 mmHg' and a one-line equation PAO₂ = FiO₂ × 713 − PaCO₂/0.8, linking to the alv lesson.

what: Teach net acid production: fruit and vegetables supply organic anions (alkali) that offset part of the protein acid load; this is why net endogenous acid production ≈ 1 mmol/kg is diet-dependent and explains CKD diet advice.
fix: One sentence plus a key 'Diet alters fixed acid'.

what: Align with BTS/SIGN asthma severity: PaCO₂ 4.6–6.0 kPa is life-threatening, > 6.0 kPa near-fatal. 48 mmHg (6.4 kPa) is 'near-fatal asthma', a term MRCEM uses.
evidence: BTS/SIGN British guideline on the management of asthma.
fix: Explanation: '48 mmHg (6.4 kPa) is near-fatal asthma: call ICU.'

what: Mention why 1.34 (vs 1.39 theoretical Hüfner) and that CO-Hb and MetHb lower content with a normal PaO₂; link to the co-oximetry lesson.
fix: Add one bullet under 'Which lever matters?'.

what: Note that P/F changes with PEEP, FiO₂ and altitude (Berlin adjusts for altitude: P/F × barometric pressure/760), so a single P/F can mislead.
fix: Add a 'Limits of P/F' bullet.

what: (6) Lessons are not mapped to exam blueprints.
fix: Add an 'Exam' filter on Learn (MRCEM Primary physiology: modules 1–5, 7; MRCEM SBA: 8–10; USMLE Step 1: 1–5, 9; Step 2: 9–13) and a 'High-yield for my exam' path.
